title: Project Life Cycle, Appraisal, Feasibility and Viability (PMT 801)
subject: Project management
description: Thirty questions across easy, medium and hard on the project life cycle phases, the appraisal team, feasibility indicators, feasibility studies and viability.

questions.prompt: What is appraisal, according to the lecture?
options: An analysis of opinion based on facts, expressed by an expert on a proposed project
A legal contract between client and contractor
A method of setting contractor pay
questions.explanation: The opinion does not have to be very accurate, but its reliability depends on the appraiser and on the data used.

questions.prompt: What basic question does a feasibility study ask?
questions.explanation: Feasibility means possibility. The question of whether it should be done belongs to viability.

questions.prompt: What does viability look at?
options: Whether the project is technically possible
Necessity and economic desirability, asking whether the project should be done
questions.explanation: Viability goes on to cost, benefits and their relationship in line with the decision maker's goals.

questions.prompt: How many feasibility indicators does the lecture list?
questions.explanation: They are technological, economic, legal, financial, physical and socio-political indicators.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the six feasibility indicators?
questions.explanation: Physical indicators cover climate, soil type and regional topography.

questions.prompt: Which four phases appear in the life cycle activities table?
questions.explanation: Each phase has its own list of activities.

questions.prompt: Which phase records the bulk of construction, with more than 80 percent of the total implementation effort?
questions.explanation: The execution phase also attracts the general public, for example when sites are cleared and equipment is moved.

questions.prompt: Who coordinates the appraisal team?
questions.explanation: The project manager welds together the data supplied by the other professionals into an appraisal report.

questions.prompt: Which technique is described as a balance sheet of the long-run and short-run costs and benefits of economic and social projects?
questions.explanation: The lecture's examples include dualising a major motorway and weighing the value of lives saved.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture describe a feasibility study in relation to the investment decision?
options: As a binding order the investor must follow
As a means to arrive at an investment decision, which need not agree with the study's conclusions
As an end in itself that replaces the decision
questions.explanation: It would be rare to find an investor response that conforms fully to a study.

questions.prompt: Why is the conception phase called the main engine of project success, although it takes little space on the graph?
options: It uses most of the project's resources
It is when construction takes place
It is the only phase the public sees
Careless conception can mark the beginning of failure, abandonment or collapse
questions.explanation: Conception data must account for time of commencement, inflation, exchange rates, interest rates, politics and government policy.

questions.prompt: What does the lecture say about a doubtful project idea at conception and planning?
options: It is better to collapse the idea there than to execute with manipulated conception and planning data
Execute it anyway and adjust later
Wait until after the execution phase to decide
Hide the weakness from the client
questions.explanation: At those phases a project idea can be collapsed without any issue of success, failure or abandonment.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture distinguish execution cost from total project cost?
options: Execution cost includes all four phases
Total project cost is the sum of conception, planning, execution and termination costs, and execution cost is only one part of it
questions.explanation: Execution is the biggest part, but it is not the whole cost.

questions.prompt: Which professional is primarily concerned with site analysis and the highest and best use of the client's land?
questions.explanation: The estate surveyor and valuer also appraises the marketability and maintainability of the project.

questions.prompt: What does the architect determine in the appraisal team?
options: The best site value for the project
Whether the proposed project is designable, and the sketch and specifications used for the material market survey
The demand and supply of the national economy
questions.explanation: The accountant handles budgeting and funding, and the economist handles the economy.

questions.prompt: Which example shows appraisal used for project evaluation and performance?
options: An investor asking whether to expand or contract after investing
A client deciding how much to invest
A client deciding where to invest
A state deciding on a metro line before spending
questions.explanation: The first purpose is pre-investment decision, and the second is evaluating the performance of an existing investment.

questions.prompt: Which question belongs to the economic indicator?
options: Is it legally possible to invest in a project of that size?
Considering soil and climate, is it physically possible?
Are the funds available to execute it?
Can the nation's economy sustain a project such as a nuclear power plant at this time?
questions.explanation: The other options belong to the legal, physical and financial indicators.

questions.prompt: What does the chain image say about the feasibility indicators?
options: The indicators are added up and averaged
If the answer to any indicator is no, the appraisal stops there
Negative answers are overruled by the client
questions.explanation: Like a chain, one broken hook stops it working.

questions.prompt: What does 'viability starts where feasibility stops' mean?
options: There is no overlap, and feasibility must stop positively before viability begins
Both are done together at the same time
questions.explanation: If feasibility does not stop positively, it is futile to go into viability.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between conclusive viability and compelling viability?
options: Conclusive viability compels action, and compelling viability only advises
The professional advises on viability (conclusive), and the client who decides compels action (compelling)
Both are decided by the professional
Both are decided by the client alone
questions.explanation: The professional can only advise and cannot compel action.

questions.prompt: How does the lecture say suppliers of equipment or technology sometimes misuse the term feasibility study?
options: They use it only for legal documents
They base it entirely on local conditions
They call an outline oriented to supplying equipment or particular techniques a feasibility study
They apply it only to government projects
questions.explanation: Such studies can mislead and result in the misapplication of resources.

questions.prompt: Why can studies based on experience in industrial countries mislead in a developing country?
options: They are not adapted to local production factors and conditions, which can cause resources to be misapplied
questions.explanation: A feasibility study must relate to available production factors and the local market and production conditions, translated into cost and income.

questions.prompt: A study identifies a market served by an investment of about ₦13 million, but the investor decides to invest ₦5 million. What follows?
options: A revised feasibility study is needed for the lower outlay, reusing many parameters from the original
The original study stays valid unchanged
A completely new study is needed with nothing reused
questions.explanation: The revision does not need the same volume of work, but the final investment differs substantially from the first study.

questions.prompt: A feasibility study may be which of the following?
options: Market-oriented or based on materials inputs
questions.explanation: It takes its initiative from an assumed or existing demand, or from available materials or energy.

questions.prompt: If the data show a non-viable project, what should the feasibility study do?
options: Adjust the parameters, programme, material inputs and technology to try to present a viable project, and if it is still not viable, say so and justify it
questions.explanation: The study should describe this optimisation process and justify the assumptions and solutions.

questions.prompt: Why must the scope of the project be defined unequivocally in a feasibility study?
options: Because scope has no effect on costs
To avoid appointing a project manager
Because only drawings are legally binding
Final estimates of costs and profitability are only meaningful if the scope is clear, ideally set out in drawings and schedules
questions.explanation: Defining scope clearly also makes sure no essential part or cost is omitted.

questions.prompt: How are appraisals styled in Nigeria?
options: As pre-investment studies called feasibility and viability studies
questions.explanation: An appraisal is made up of feasibility and viability studies.

questions.prompt: A state government wants an underground metro to ease Lagos traffic. What does the lecture say is needed?
options: A comprehensive feasibility and viability study on social, economic, political and financial parameters
No study, since it is a government project
questions.explanation: A project of this size is where the real involvement of an appraiser is needed.

questions.prompt: On what does the reliability of an appraiser's opinion depend?
options: The appraiser's qualification and experience, and the quality and accuracy of the data analysed
The size of the client's land only
questions.explanation: The opinion does not need to be very accurate, but it is a function of both the expert and the data.

questions.prompt: Which set of items belongs under the financial evaluation in the feasibility study summary?
options: Net present value, internal rate of return, pay-back period, simple rate of return, break-even analysis and sensitivity analysis
questions.explanation: The summary also covers background, market, materials, location, engineering, manpower, implementation scheduling and conclusions.
